claim: `overEachFile` at check/modules/change-walking/change-walking.module.code.ts read every path a change carries through `bodiesIn` before handing the bytes to a judge that dropped the path. At audit the change is the whole tree, so a check judging TypeScript alone opened every image and every log first. It now takes the path test its judge held and applies that test before the read, as `overEveryIn` beside it already did. Over one tree of 378,949 files the seven checks on that route fell from 3,976,089 read calls and 13.52 GB to 2,118,825 calls and 2.64 GB, and from 31.5 processor seconds to 25.1. file-is-owned-by-a-page judges a path by its name alone and never looks at the bytes it opens, so filtering bought that one nothing.

evidence:
Read 2026-09-19 from the cost rows each check keeps at check/code/pages/<slug>/<slug>.check-code.audit.logs.uncommitted.jsonl, for the audit at 4081530b30fb352eacc0a51fd15be8f5cfee35f7, and measured again either side of 1a907eb5d744cd10f4a929a09676594a11eae56f.

The two routes. `overEachFile` called `bodiesIn`, which called `change.after(path)` for every path in `change.changed`. That `after` is `onDisk`, a plain `readFileSync`. The judge `overEach` builds opens with `if (!taken(given.path)) return []`, so the path test ran with the bytes already in hand. `overEveryIn` tests `taken(path)` before it calls `textIn`. `overEachFile` now takes that same test as an argument, and each of its nine callers hands over the test its judge held.

What the reading route cost on the audit round at 4081530b30f:

  require-import-extension            14.040s    454,885 reads   1.24 GB
  file-is-owned-by-a-page              4.977s    476,066 reads   1.25 GB
  page-named-as-stated                 9.119s    456,141 reads   1.24 GB
  no-rule-in-two-files                29.290s  1,199,773 reads   1.53 GB
  change-is-reached-through-a-runner   6.858s    453,056 reads   1.24 GB
  no-relative-specifier                5.746s    453,023 reads   1.24 GB
  popover-keeps-its-viewport-cap       9.567s    459,459 reads   1.25 GB

What each check spent before the change and after it, run alone over the whole tree at 378,945 files and then at 378,949, counting syscr and rchar off /proc/self/io and process.cpuUsage() around the audit entry point:

  require-import-extension            457,695 / 181,853 reads   1.89 / 0.10 GB    6.90 / 5.75s
  file-is-owned-by-a-page             479,007 / 479,007 reads   1.89 / 1.89 GB    2.25 / 2.28s
  page-named-as-stated                458,925 / 158,296 reads   1.89 / 0.06 GB    4.05 / 3.07s
  no-rule-in-two-files              1,206,478 / 930,693 reads   2.18 / 0.39 GB   10.59 / 9.42s
  change-is-reached-through-a-runner  455,868 / 180,048 reads   1.89 / 0.10 GB    2.79 / 1.77s
  no-relative-specifier               455,836 / 180,014 reads   1.89 / 0.10 GB    2.35 / 1.45s
  popover-keeps-its-viewport-cap      462,280 /   8,914 reads   1.90 / 0.01 GB    2.60 / 1.37s
  the seven                         3,976,089 / 2,118,825     13.52 / 2.64 GB    31.5 / 25.1s

A second round after the change answered within 0.03% on every count. This tree holds more uncommitted log than the tree at 4081530b30f did, which is why its before is 13.52 GB where that round read 9.00, and the machine was quieter, which is why 31.5 processor seconds where that round spent 79.6. Each pair is what the change bought, and the two rounds do not compare with one another.

Bytes fell four fifths where read calls fell half, because what went was the logs and the images and what is left is TypeScript. Processor seconds fell a fifth, because parsing the TypeScript a check keeps is most of what that check spends.

file-is-owned-by-a-page is flat because it judges every path: it reads a path's name and never looks at the bytes. Opening them is what tells it a folder, or a path gone since the tree was listed, so dropping that read would change what it answers. It now makes 1.89 GB of the 2.64 GB the seven read.

What this is not. The tree grew 4.6% in the eight hours before that audit round, from 362,097 files at cb9262884a2 to 378,917 at 4081530b30f, so what a check spends rises with the tree whichever route that check takes. Filtering first does not stop that rise, it divides it.

Left unmeasured. Whether one tree read shared by every check would beat several filtered reads. What such a read would cost in the change phase, where a check is handed a few paths rather than the whole tree. Whether no-rule-in-two-files, which read 1.53 GB over 1,199,773 calls where its six neighbours read 1.24 GB over 453,000, is paying for its own tree search rather than for this — filtering left that gap where it was, at 930,693 calls for 0.39 GB against 180,000 calls for 0.10 GB.
